passage: Tuesday: at the park gate Pema, two, screamed when her father, Varun, said it was time to go. Two weeks later, Pema's mother and grandmother said the same short no to the biscuit tin, and Varun said it too. Later, at the shop, Pema reached for the toffees. "Not today," said Varun. She sighed, dropped her hand and went to pat the shop dog. "Thank you for listening, Pema," he said quietly. The next morning she cried at the gate again, and he stayed calm.

qa.q: Where did Pema scream when Varun said it was time to go?
qa.a: She screamed at the park gate.

qa.q: What did Pema's sigh at the shop show about how she took the no?
qa.a: It showed she had accepted the no this time. She felt a little disappointed but let it go and moved on to the dog.

qa.q: Why did Varun stay calm when Pema cried at the gate again the next morning?
qa.a: Acceptance does not come every time, so he expected it. He kept the limit steady and did not treat her tears as a failure.

qa.q: How does it help Pema that her mother, grandmother and Varun all give the same short no?
qa.a: She hears one clear rule from everyone, so there is nothing to test or bargain over. That makes it easier for her to accept.

grounding: After many calm, consistent limits the toddler sometimes hears no, sighs and moves on, and is quietly praised without expecting it every time.

"Papa, phone?" Ojas, two, reached for it.

"No phone, Ojas," Ujjwal said calmly.

Ojas sighed a big sigh. "Okay." He went back to his puzzle.

Ujjwal's brother raised his eyebrows. "He usually screams."

"Not always," Ujjwal said quietly. Then to Ojas: "Thank you for listening."

Ojas grinned and fitted another piece.

qa.q: What did Ojas go back to?
qa.a: Ojas went back to his puzzle.

qa.q: What does Ojas's big sigh suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Ojas felt a little disappointed but accepting, having heard no many times before.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal respond to Ojas accepting the no?
qa.a: He praised it quietly, without making a fuss or expecting it every time.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal's brother see Ojas's calm response?
qa.a: The brother is surprised, since Ojas usually screams.

grounding: Shows a toddler accepting a no after consistent limits, with a parent who praises it quietly.

passage:
Grandmother's note, Tuesday.

Madhuri, two, wanted more biscuits. Her mother, Shreya, said, "No more, Madhuri." I said the same when she asked me.

Madhuri paused, sighed and said, "Okay," then went to her dolls.

Shreya smiled at me and said quietly to Madhuri, "Good listening." Yesterday she cried at the same no, and we didn't expect this every day.

qa.q: What did Madhuri want more of?
What was Madhuri feeling when she sighed and said "Okay"?
qa.a: Madhuri felt a little disappointed but calm and accepting.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri accept the no this time?
qa.a: Both her mother and grandmother gave the same calm limit, and that consistency builds acceptance.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel after Madhuri moved on?
qa.a: Shreya likely feels pleased and thankful for the grandmother's support.

grounding: Shows a toddler sometimes accepting a no after calm, consistent limits from every adult, with quiet praise.
